title: Underpromotion: when a knight or rook beats the queen
outcomes: Finds the promotion to a knight that gives check and attacks a second piece
Chooses a rook or a knight where a queen would stalemate
Checks the queen promotion first and says why it fails
Says when the queen is simply right

steps.text: When a pawn reaches the last rank, you choose its new piece. The queen is the usual choice because it is strongest. Sometimes another piece is better. A **knight** can give check and attack a second piece at once. A **rook** can win where a queen would leave the opponent with no legal move and no check: **stalemate**, a draw. Choosing a weaker piece on purpose is **underpromotion**.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has a queen on d7; the pawn on b7 is about to promote.

line.say: Underpromotion: a knight. It gives check to the king on a6 and attacks the queen on d7.
The king must move. Nothing can capture the knight on b8.
The knight takes the queen. The tablebase says White wins this position.

claims.statement: A knight on b8 attacks a6 (the king) and d7 (the queen).
No black piece can capture a knight on b8, so the king must move.
Promoting to a knight keeps the win (tablebase).

steps.text:
Check the queen first. Ask two questions.
**Does the queen promotion fail?** It might stalemate, or it might be captured at once.
**Does a knight on that square give check and attack a second piece?** As with any fork (*L-TAC-FORK-1*), ask whether the knight can be captured and whether the second target is worth taking.
*Rule of thumb:* the queen is the default. These questions find the exceptions.

steps.title: Does the knight still fork?
steps.prompt: In the second position Black's rook has moved from d7 to b7. In the third, no pawn can promote. Predict, then check.
Which part is least clear: seeing the knight fork, seeing the stalemate, or deciding that the queen is simply right?
